auditCorrections.finding: The record is dated 2023-10-30 with basis 'signature', where the document version holds only publishedAt 2023-11-01 and the schema requires a provision claim to carry one of the edition's own dates; and the statement's 'to plan and implement the Department of Energy's AI model evaluation tools and AI testbeds' implies a duty to implement the tools themselves.

Verified in the cached Federal Register print: Sec. 4.1(b) opens 'Within 270 days of the date of this order' and reads 'shall develop and, to the extent permitted by law and available appropriations, implement a plan for developing the Department of Energy's AI model evaluation tools and AI testbeds'. auditCorrections.finding: The statement's 'automate development of other such models' drops 'and deployment', and omitting the list's residual item ('give rise to other risks identified by AISI') presents an open list as closed.
auditCorrections.disposition: Applied. Verified in the cached memorandum: the sentence ends 'automate development and deployment of other models with such capabilities, and give rise to other risks identified by AISI'. The statement now tracks the whole list, the quoted evidence item carries the sentence whole instead of stopping at 'chemical weapons', and the qualification says the list is not closed. The compression of 'the Secretary of Commerce, acting through AISI within NIST' to the institute is kept, as the quoted sentence reads 'AISI shall pursue', and the evidence note now says so.

auditCorrections.finding: The statement drops the page's 'SI' twice, reporting a general remit where the page states one scoped to the systems the centre is named for; and the cache metadata shows the request was redirected from /caisi to /caissi, which the record does not say.
auditCorrections.disposition: Applied. Verified in the cached page: 'Establish voluntary agreements with private sector SI developers and evaluators, and lead unclassified evaluations of SI capabilities that may pose risks to national security.' Both 'SI' are restored to the statement, the scoped second limb is added as a quoted evidence item and the whole sentence as an explicit paraphrase (the page's quotation budget is about 38 words), and the qualification records that 'SI' is the page's own abbreviation. Verified the redirect in the cache metadata (requestedUrl https://www.nist.gov/caisi, finalUrl https://www.nist.gov/caissi, HTTP 200) and recorded it in the qualification, with no relation inferred between the two names.

auditCorrections.finding: The statement's framing is not the Annex's (it is headed as criteria for designating general-purpose AI models with systemic risk under Article 51, and its opening speaks of determining capabilities or an impact equivalent to those in Article 51(1)(a)), and a three-word parenthetical is thin as the only quote for a provision claim.
auditCorrections.disposition: Applied. Verified in the cached Official Journal text: the Annex is headed 'Criteria for the designation of general-purpose AI models with systemic risk referred to in Article 51' and opens 'For the purpose of determining that a general-purpose AI model has capabilities or an impact equivalent to those set out in Article 51(1), point (a), the Commission shall take into account the following criteria'; point (d) reads 'the input and output modalities of the model, such as text to text (large language models), text to image, multi-modality, and the state of the art thresholds for determining high-impact capabilities for each modality, and the specific type of inputs and outputs (e.g. biological sequences)'. auditCorrections.disposition: Applied. Verified paragraph 5 in the cached document, across the page break: the sentence carries all three limbs. object.value: Purpose of the section on AI and CBRN threats, with a particular focus on biological weapons (Sec. 4.4(a))

claims.statement: Section 4.4 of Executive Order 14110, headed "Reducing Risks at the Intersection of AI and CBRN Threats", states that the actions it directs are to better understand and mitigate the risk of AI being misused to assist in the development or use of CBRN threats, with a particular focus on biological weapons.

time.note: Dated by the order's signature; the subsections it introduces carry their own deadlines.

claims.qualification: States the order's own purpose for this section. It is not evidence that any action was taken under it, and it names no AI system. claims.subject: us-eo-14110-2023

object.value: Evaluation of the potential for AI to be misused to enable CBRN threats, within 180 days (Sec. 4.4(a)(i))

claims.statement: Section 4.4(a)(i) of Executive Order 14110 directs the Secretary of Homeland Security, within 180 days and in consultation with the Secretary of Energy and the Director of OSTP, to evaluate the potential for AI to be misused to enable the development or production of CBRN threats while also considering AI's benefits and application in countering them, consulting experts from the Department of Energy, private AI laboratories, academia and third-party model evaluators.

time.note: Dated by the order's signature; the directive runs 180 days from that date.

claims.qualification: A directive to an agency head. No record is made that the evaluation was carried out, and the order names no AI laboratory or evaluator. The same subsection requires a report to the President with recommendations, which is not separately recorded in this pass. Executive Order 14110 was revoked by Executive Order 14148 of 20 January 2025 (dataset record fl-us-eo14110-revoked).

object.value: Contracted National Academies study on AI and biosecurity risks (Sec. 4.4(a)(ii))

claims.statement: Section 4.4(a)(ii) of Executive Order 14110 directs the Secretary of Defense, within 120 days, to contract with the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine for a study that assesses the ways in which AI can increase biosecurity risks, including risks from generative AI models trained on biological data, and that makes recommendations on mitigating them.

object.value: Department of Energy evaluation tools for biological and other threat outputs, and model guardrails (Sec. 4.1(b))

claims.statement: Working paper BWC/MSP/2025/WP.4, submitted by the United Kingdom to the 2025 Meeting of States Parties to the Biological Weapons Convention, proposes artificial intelligence and digital technology as a technical theme for the Convention's science and technology review mechanism, stating that the mechanism could explore the opportunities and risks of AI within the life sciences and the potential for layering AI into the Convention to strengthen implementation and operationalisation.

time.note: Date on the document itself; the UNODA documents list gives a submit date of 21 April 2026 for the same symbol, and the meeting sat in Geneva on 15-17 December 2025. Both dates are stated and neither is reconciled here.

claims.qualification: A proposal in a working paper submitted by one State Party. It is not a decision of the Meeting of States Parties, and no mechanism, theme or outcome is recorded as agreed.

evidence.locator: Section on proposed technical themes, point (b) "Artificial Intelligence and Digital Tech", PDF p. 4
evidence.passage: The S&T Review Mechanism could explore the opportunities and risks of AI within the life sciences, and the potential for layering AI into the BTWC to strengthen implementation and operationalisation.
evidence.note: The same point states that AI and digital tech can act as a foundation for innovation and a catalyst for other technologies such as robotics, bioinformatics and synthesis.

claims.subject: bwc-msp-2025-wp4

object.value: Timeline entry for 2021: protein-structure prediction as both accelerating research and raising governance needs

claims.statement: Working paper BWC/MSP/2025/WP.4, submitted by the United Kingdom to the 2025 Meeting of States Parties, states in its fifty-year timeline of life-science advances that the AlphaFold protein-folding prediction database published by DeepMind in 2021 accelerated scientific research in fields such as drug discovery but also demonstrated potential for misuse, highlighting the importance of stronger guard rails and AI governance.

time.note: Date on the document itself; the paper dates the AlphaFold database entry to 2021.

claims.qualification: What one State Party's working paper states in a historical timeline, with its own footnoted sources, which were not retrieved. It is not a finding about any system's capability, and the record does not reproduce the paper's characterisation of what the technology could do beyond the general words used here.
claims.hazardNote: The paper's wording about what protein design could enable was paraphrased as "potential for misuse" rather than quoted, so that no capability detail is reproduced; only the governance clause is quoted.

evidence.locator: Timeline of scientific and technological advances, entry for 2021, PDF p. 3
evidence.passage: highlighting the importance of stronger guard rails and AI governance
evidence.note: Explicit paraphrase of the rest of the entry: in 2021 DeepMind published the AlphaFold database, an artificial intelligence programme for protein folding prediction, which accelerated scientific research in fields such as drug discovery but, the paper says, also showed a potential for misuse.

claims.subject: bwc-msp-2025-wp14

object.value: Stated position: AI among technologies that can aid Convention verification and implementation, with a call to other States Parties

claims.statement: The statement by the United States issued as document BWC/MSP/2025/WP.14 at the 2025 Meeting of States Parties states that advanced and emerging technologies, including AI, can aid Biological Weapons Convention verification and implementation and help stop dangerous dual-use biological research, and calls on every State Party to join its efforts to seek ways in which AI and other tools can help verify Convention compliance, enhance transparency and strengthen the collective ability of States Parties to detect, defend against and respond to biological threats.

time.note: Date on the document; the 2025 Meeting of States Parties sat in Geneva on 15-17 December 2025. The document is marked as issued without formal editing.

claims.qualification: A statement of one State Party's position, recorded as what the document says. It is not a decision of the Meeting, not a described method, and not evidence that AI aids verification, that any technology has been used for it, or that any State Party joined the call; the statement's assertions about other States Parties are not recorded. The call is addressed to other States Parties, which no instrument requires of them, so the provision kind is the risk and subject domain of the passage rather than a required action; whether states_provision suits a national statement at all is an open question for the maintainer.

evidence.passage: Advanced and emerging technologies, including AI, can aid BWC verification and implementation and help stop dangerous dual-use biological research.

evidence.locator: Paragraph 5, across the page break (PDF pp. 1-2)
evidence.passage: we call on every State … Party to join us in our efforts to seek ways in which AI and other tools can help us verify BWC compliance, enhance transparency, and strengthen our collective ability to detect, defend against, and respond to biological threats
evidence.note: The sentence whole, across the page break; the ellipsis stands where the page footnote marker and running head interrupt it in the PDF text layer.

claims.subject: bwc-msp-2025-wp27

object.value: Stated position: biotechnology and AI used as new kinds of weapons of war among novel and hybrid threats

claims.statement: The statement by the United Kingdom issued as document BWC/MSP/2025/WP.27 at the 2025 Meeting of States Parties states that technology is at present outstripping diplomacy and that novel and hybrid threats to collective security have emerged, including using biotechnology and AI as new kinds of weapons of war.

time.note: Date on the document; the 2025 Meeting of States Parties sat in Geneva on 15-17 December 2025.

claims.qualification: A statement of one State Party's position, in its own general wording. It names no actor, no system and no incident, and it is not a finding that any such use has occurred.

evidence.passage: At present, technology is outstripping diplomacy. Novel and hybrid threats to our collective security have emerged, including using biotechnology and AI as new kinds of weapons of war.
evidence.note: The paragraph continues that these threats come in many different forms and from many different quarters.

claims.subject: bwc-msp-2025-wp28

object.value: Stated position: genome editing, synthetic biology and AI as beneficial but, if misused, able to lead to biological weapons production

claims.statement: The statement by Japan issued as document BWC/MSP/2025/WP.28 at the 2025 Meeting of States Parties states that new technologies such as genome editing technology, synthetic biology and artificial intelligence offer great benefits to humanity but, if misused, could lead to the production of biological weapons that cause devastating harm, and that there are growing concerns that these technologies are becoming available to a wider range of actors.

time.note: Date on the document; the 2025 Meeting of States Parties sat in Geneva on 15-17 December 2025.

claims.qualification: A statement of one State Party's position, in its own conditional wording. It names no system, no actor and no capability level, and it is not a finding that any technology has been misused.

evidence.passage: New technologies such as genome editing technology, synthetic biology, and artificial intelligence offer great benefits to humanity; however, if misused, they could lead to the production of biological weapons that cause devastating harm.
evidence.note: The paragraph continues that there are growing concerns that these technologies are becoming available to a wider range of actors, increasing the risk of proliferation of biological weapons.

openQuestions.question: Auditor A asks, for all three Biological Weapons Convention records (ab-gov-bwc-us-wp14-ai-verification, ab-gov-bwc-uk-wp27-biotech-ai-threats, ab-gov-bwc-japan-wp28-misuse-risk), whether states_provision suits a national statement at all: the predicate's description is about an exact framework edition stating one provision.
openQuestions.recommended: Decide before admission. A national statement is not an instrument's provision; the honest options are a new predicate for a position stated in a document submitted to a treaty meeting, or recording these as propositions in the arguments strand with the document as the text that articulates them. The three records now use provision kind 'risk_domain' consistently, which keeps them readable either way, and none of them says that any State Party acted.

openQuestions.question: Is the national security memorandum of 24 October 2024 still in force? Executive Order 14179 of 23 January 2025 directs a review of actions taken pursuant to Executive Order 14110, which the memorandum says it fulfils, but no revocation or replacement of the memorandum was retrieved in this pass.
openQuestions.recommended: Record the memorandum's provisions as stated and dated, with no status beyond issuance (as done here), and task a short follow-up search of 2025-2026 presidential documents and whitehouse.gov for a replacing national security memorandum before any admission. Do not infer revocation from the revocation of Executive Order 14110.

openQuestions.question: How should the NIST centre named on the page retrieved here (Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence, CAISSI) relate to the Center for AI Standards and Innovation (CAISI) and the U.S. AI Safety Institute already in the dataset?
openQuestions.recommended: Keep them as separate identifiers until a naming announcement is retrieved, and record any link with the name_transition_announced predicate in a separate task. This pack's record cites only what the page states about the centre's evaluation focus.

openQuestions.question: BWC/MSP/2025/WP.4 carries 10 December 2025 on its face but a submit date of 21 April 2026 in the UNODA documents list. Which date should a record use?
openQuestions.recommended: Date the record by the document's own date (as done here) and keep the list's submit date in the document's dateNote, since the document date is the expression's own and the list date may reflect UN processing.

openQuestions.question: Should national statements delivered at a Biological Weapons Convention meeting and issued as working papers (WP.14, WP.27, WP.28 here) be recorded as documents of the submitting State Party, with a published or signed_commitment claim, rather than only as provision records on the document?
openQuestions.recommended: Record them as document versions with states_provision claims, as here, because the available predicates for publication take an organisation or public body as subject and this pack creates no country entities. If the maintainer wants attribution to States Parties, add country entities and a publication predicate in a later task.

openQuestions.question: Two records in this draft are bounded negative records about documents that the dataset already treats as central (Executive Order 14409 and the EU AI Act). Are they wanted in a candidate pack?
openQuestions.recommended: Keep both: each states its search terms, scope and date, and both answer a research question this pack poses (where biological risk is and is not named in current instruments). They are flagged for the cross-family check as inferred and negative records.
